annotation.notes: Retro-annotated from docs/evaluation.md §3.15, an independent blind pass with no memory of this project's own findings — the third of three untested deep-tier runtime references (JVM, Rust, .NET) closed by this round, and the only one of the four second-batch repositories with a pinned commit in the source record. A hardcoded JWT signing key committed to source (SEC-001, Confirmed/High risk) was also found and filed under Kind: Security, out of the performance rubric per SKILL.md Hard Rule 8 — not encoded here, since this schema's category enum has no security axis. `forbidden` is intentionally empty: §3.15 notes the review correctly did NOT explain PERF-001/PERF-003 as a sync-over-async deadlock (ASP.NET Core installs no request SynchronizationContext, ruling that mechanism out) — but this is a mechanism-attribution nuance on a real finding, not a separately-located candidate that should not be reported, so it does not fit this schema's forbidden-item shape without fabricating a location for it.

expected.mechanism: Every request, read or write, is wrapped by this pipeline behavior in a call to ConduitContext.BeginTransaction()/CommitTransaction() (src/Conduit/Infrastructure/ConduitContext.cs:94-133), which invoke the SYNCHRONOUS Database.BeginTransaction()/.Commit()/.Rollback() -- not their *Async equivalents -- from inside an async ValueTask<TResponse> Handle(...) method. Applied globally: two genuinely blocking DB round trips on literally every endpoint, including plain GET reads that need no transaction at all, each occupying a thread-pool thread for the round-trip duration and holding a pooled connection open for the full handler.

Unconditionally .Include(x => x.ArticleFavorites)s the full favoriting-user join table for every article returned by the list and detail endpoints, only to discard every row but a count -- Article.FavoritesCount/Favorited read ArticleFavorites.Count off the materialized in-memory collection instead of a count query. Cost scales with how many people ever favorited an article, not with page size, so it grows without bound as the app is used, on the two most-hit reads in the service.

Calls the synchronous queryable.Count() (not CountAsync) inside the same async handler, on the already-filtered IQueryable, to compute ArticlesCount for pagination -- a second blocking DB round trip re-executing every WHERE clause already applied to the page query.

Loops over the caller-supplied TagList and, for each unrecognized tag, issues FindAsync then an immediate SaveChangesAsync -- a round-trip pair per new tag, per article creation. TagList has no length validation in ArticleDataValidator, so the round-trip count is attacker-controlled, not merely inefficient.
